title: "The Full Use of Your Powers Along the Lines of Excellence"
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. uses a JFK address to 1963 White House student participants to illuminate the philosophical foundation of his classroom Everest statement: that learning is not merely preparation for life but the full enactment of human powers toward excellence. JFK's Greek-derived definition of happiness as 'the full use of your powers along the lines of excellence' becomes Stuart's framework for articulating why knowledge, strength, and ability growth in history, government, and English is not merely instrumental but inherently joyful and meaningful. The article functions as an invitation for colleagues to bring this orienting language directly into tomorrow's class.
points: JFK's formulation of happiness as 'the full use of your powers along the lines of excellence' gives teachers a philosophically grounded, student-accessible language for the purpose of academic work.
The Everest Statement — a class-specific articulation of what students are growing toward — is the pedagogical translation of JFK's idea into daily classroom practice.
Growth in knowledge, strength, and ability is not merely preparation for future goals; according to this framework it is intrinsically joyful and meaningful in itself.
Bringing a primary-source text — a JFK speech — into a teaching moment about learning models the very disciplinary practice that the course is designed to develop.
The article's concision functions as its argument: the JFK idea is complete enough to stand on its own and be applied in tomorrow's class without elaborate mediation.
quotes: In June I went on a PD adventure to BC High, an all-boys school in Boston. While I was there, I noticed the JFK Presidential Library was in walking distance and, having time to spare, I made the trip. My favorite takeaways from the library were a couple JFK one-liners.

I can assure you that there is no career which you will adopt when you leave college that will bring you a more and greater sense of satisfaction and a greater feeling of participation in a great effort than will your work here or in your state or in your community. [T]his generation of Americans — you here who will be in positions of responsibility for the rest of this century — will deal with the most difficult, sensitive, and dangerous problems that any society of people has ever dealt with at any age.

The Greeks defined happiness as the full use of your powers along the lines of excellence, and I can imagine no place where you can use your powers more fully along lines more excellent in the 1960's than to be in the service of the United States. Happiness, according to JFK and the Greeks he's referencing, is 'the full use of your powers along the lines of excellence.'
That is basically what learning in any subject is about. That's the goal of my history courses this year, my government course this year, and the English courses I've taught throughout my career.

Between lines of this Everest statement is an idea: seeking to grow one's knowledge, strength, and ability is a fundamentally enjoyable, meaningful, and joyful endeavor. There is a goodness one feels when being together with a group of people whose minds and hearts are set on such things.
